summary: HERMES is an interactive crew health monitoring prototype for long-duration space missions. It brings together 26 simulated health and cabin measurements, personal well-being and vision check-ins, and mission-wide alerts in a single dashboard. Astronauts can review the whole crew, investigate changes in individual readings, and ask an on-demand AI assistant to explain what the data shows. Four selectable scenarios let users practise recognising issues and deciding what to verify next. HERMES demonstrates how a crew could assess a developing situation independently when immediate support from Earth is unavailable.
details:
From a crew alert to the underlying evidence

When an alert appears, the first questions are practical. Who is affected? Which reading changed? Has it been changing for a while? We built HERMES around that sequence. The crew overview shows the current status of three fictional astronauts and highlights active alerts. Selecting a crew member opens their readings and trends, while the mission alerts remain visible across every view. The history and statistics panel lets users review recorded measurements over a chosen time range and export them as CSV for further analysis.


HOW IT WORKS

Rehearsing realistic monitoring decisions

The simulator provides four scenarios: nominal operations, exertion during extravehicular activity, low cabin oxygen, and elevated temperature with increased radiation. Users can apply a scenario to one astronaut and watch the readings shift gradually. For example, in the low-oxygen scenario, the crew can follow blood oxygen saturation and cabin oxygen together, identify the affected astronaut, and inspect the trend behind the rule-based alert. Each scenario gives the crew a repeatable way to practise interpreting readings and deciding what to verify.

Tracking changes from a personal baseline

The check-in adds information that telemetry alone cannot capture. Crew members can record how they feel, complete a short reaction-time task, and use a visual distortion grid and a letter-orientation test. HERMES compares recorded results with the individual's baseline and surfaces changes for review. These activities and alert thresholds are designed for prototype evaluation and training. They require clinical validation before any operational use.

An assistant that responds on request

The HERMES Crew AI Assistant is available from every view, and the conversation stays open as users navigate. On request, it can summarise the crew's status, answer a question about a particular astronaut, or suggest which recorded readings to verify. It uses recent telemetry, statistics, and available check-in results as context. The model runs on the host computer through Ollama. Mission alerts are evaluated independently by explicit rules, so the crew can continue to use the dashboard when the assistant is unavailable.

What the demonstration shows

Next steps

We plan to integrate real sensor inputs and evaluate the interface in analogue mission exercises for further improovement. We would measure how accurately the data is helping the crew, explain the evidence behind an alert, and choose an appropriate verification step. Work with clinical and human-factors specialists would guide the validation of screening tasks, alert thresholds, and overall health check automation.

Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

HERMES uses Llama 3.2 through Ollama to generate answers and crew summaries when a user requests them. We used OpenAI Codex and ChatGPT to assist with software development, the demonstration materials, and editing this submission.
